content: Sickle cell disease is a group of genetic disorders affecting hemoglobin, with pain being the most prominent symptom due to the blockage of small blood vessels by abnormally shaped red blood cells. Other complications include chronic organ damage and priapism, which is a prolonged and painful erection of the penis. Priapism affects up to 50% of men with sickle cell disease, but there is no standardized treatment for this condition. This review aimed to evaluate the benefits and risks of various treatments for both stuttering priapism (short, repeated episodes) and fulminant priapism (lasting six hours or more) in individuals with sickle cell disease. The review included three trials involving 102 participants, conducted in outpatient settings in Jamaica, Nigeria, and the UK. These trials compared different treatments: stilboestrol versus placebo, sildenafil versus placebo, and a four-arm trial comparing ephedrine or etilefrine to placebo. The duration of these trials ranged from two weeks to six months. None of the trials measured detumescence (the resolution of an erection), which was the primary outcome of interest. However, all three trials reported on the reduction in the frequency of stuttering priapism, which was the second primary outcome. The evidence from these trials was of very low certainty, making it unclear whether stilboestrol, etilefrine, or ephedrine effectively reduce the frequency of stuttering priapism. Similarly, the evidence suggested that sildenafil may have little to no effect on reducing the frequency of stuttering priapism, but this conclusion is based on low-certainty evidence. Two trials reported on immediate side effects, but the evidence was insufficient to determine whether etilefrine or ephedrine reduce side effects. Likewise, sildenafil appeared to have little to no impact on side effects, but this conclusion is also based on low-quality evidence. All three trials were at risk of bias and involved a small number of participants, which further reduced the reliability of the findings. As a result, the overall certainty of the evidence was rated as low to very low. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine the benefits or risks of different treatments for stuttering or fulminant priapism in individuals with sickle cell disease. This highlights the urgent need for well-designed, adequately powered, multicenter randomized controlled trials to assess the effectiveness of specific interventions for priapism in this population.
